title: Glasgow Opens a Leaner Commonwealth Games as the Event Fights for Its Future
excerpt: The 23rd edition kicks off Thursday with just 10 sports across four venues — a radical downsizing that organizers say is a blueprint for survival, not a step toward extinction.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Glasgow hosts the 23rd Commonwealth Games with 3,000 athletes competing in just 10 sports.
  • India's contingent of 125 athletes faces limited medal prospects due to missing key sports.
  • Ticket sales are sluggish, with nearly 75% of sessions unsold before the opening.
  • The budget for Glasgow 2026 is £150 million, significantly lower than the £550 million spent in 2014.

The 23rd Commonwealth Games got under way in Glasgow on Thursday with an indoor opening ceremony at the OVO Hydro — a first in the event's 96-year history — as organizers bet that a radically downsized format can rescue a competition struggling for relevance in a crowded international sports calendar.

King Charles and Queen Camilla are in attendance, with the King formally declaring the Games open by reading aloud the message he placed inside the King's Baton at Buckingham Palace on Commonwealth Day in March 2025. Six-time Olympic champion Sir Chris Hoy, who carried the baton as its first bearer, is also part of the ceremony, with performances by KT Tunstall and Brit Award winner Tom Walker.

A Games Born of Crisis

This edition exists at all only because Glasgow agreed to step in after a turbulent stretch nearly killed the event. Victoria, Australia, was confirmed as host in 2022 but withdrew a year later when projected costs ballooned from A$2.6 billion to nearly A$7 billion. Malaysia was subsequently approached and also declined. Glasgow, which staged a well-regarded Games in 2014, finally agreed in late 2024 — on condition that the programme be drastically reduced.

The result is a competition spread across just four existing venues within an eight-mile corridor, with no purpose-built athletes' village. Athletes are housed in city hotels instead. The budget sits at roughly £150 million, funded largely by the £100 million in compensation paid by Victoria for its withdrawal, according to Glasgow Commonwealth Games organizers. In 2014, the city spent £550 million.

Ten Sports, 215 Medals, and Notable Absences

Only athletics, swimming, track cycling, weightlifting, 3x3 basketball, lawn bowls, netball, artistic gymnastics, judo and boxing have made the cut. Gone are badminton, hockey, cricket, squash, table tennis, triathlon, wrestling, beach volleyball and rugby sevens — a casualty list that has dismayed fans and athletes alike.

The Games will run through August 2, with 215 medal events. Para sports have been fully integrated into six disciplines, making this the largest para-sport programme in Commonwealth Games history. Two nations — Gabon and Togo — are making their debut, bringing the total to 74 competing associations, the most ever.

The return of the Commonwealth Mile, last contested in 1966, is one of the few novelties. A women's mile race has been added for the first time alongside the men's event.

Ticket Woes and Star No-Shows

Ticket sales have been sluggish. According to The Times, nearly three-quarters of the 134 scheduled sessions still had "good availability" as of last week, with only 500,000 tickets released in total — less than half the 1.2 million sold in 2014. Track cycling has sold out and only around 800 swimming tickets remained, but organizers were forced to offer complimentary tickets to Scotland Supporters Club members for events including athletics, boxing and basketball.

Top-end prices have drawn criticism. Athletics medal-session tickets at Scotstoun Stadium — which replaced the 52,000-capacity Hampden Park as the athletics venue — cost up to £150 for adults, meaning a family of four could spend over £500 for a single session. In 2014, two-thirds of tickets cost £25 or less.

Several marquee athletes have also chosen to skip Glasgow. Canadian swimmer Summer McIntosh and Australian backstroke champion Kaylee McKeown are among the notable absences. World Athletics president Sebastian Coe has repeatedly described the World Championships and Olympics as the pinnacle of track and field, a sentiment that increasingly relegates the Commonwealth Games to second-tier status.

India's Medal Hopes Take a Hit

India is fielding a 125-member squad, with Olympic javelin champion Neeraj Chopra, weightlifter Mirabai Chanu and boxer Lovlina Borgohain as the marquee names. Chanu and Borgohain will serve as flag bearers at the opening ceremony.

The country won 61 medals at Birmingham 2022, finishing fourth in the overall standings. But the absence of hockey, badminton, table tennis and wrestling — sports that have historically yielded a significant chunk of India's medal haul — means replicating that tally will be difficult. India's strongest chances are concentrated in weightlifting, boxing and athletics, with the para contingent also expected to mount a competitive campaign across powerlifting, swimming and track cycling.

Blueprint or Last Rites?

The question hanging over these Games is whether Glasgow's stripped-back model represents a sustainable future or a slow death. Phil Batty, the Glasgow 2026 chief executive, is firmly in the optimist camp.

"Glasgow has reset and reformatted the event so that the new model of the Commonwealth Games is what's going to last for the next 100 years."

— Phil Batty, CEO, Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games

Katie Sadler, CEO of the Commonwealth Games Federation, has echoed that framing, describing Glasgow 2026 as "a bridge to the Commonwealth Games of tomorrow — an exciting first step in our journey to reset and redefine the Games as a truly collaborative, flexible and sustainable model."

India's decision to host the 2030 Games in Ahmedabad — which will coincide with the event's centenary — offers the strongest argument for continued relevance. But as the Telegraph India noted, only India and Nigeria ultimately bid for 2030, raising the question of whether India secured hosting rights simply because few others wanted the financial burden.

For the Indian diaspora watching from abroad, the next 11 days in Glasgow matter beyond the medal count. The way these leaner Games are received will shape what kind of event Ahmedabad inherits in 2030 — and whether the Commonwealth Games can find a place in a world that has, in many ways, moved on from the institution that created them.
